name: Wool and merino clothes

lead: Merino is a fine, soft wool used for clothing, and people interested in smelling clean say it stays fresher than other fabrics between washes.

Odour arises from bacteria acting on sweat, and proponents believe wool limits this. Wikipedia says the Merino breed originated in the Iberian Peninsula in the High Middle Ages and that its wool is generally under 24 microns in diameter. No source reviewed compares merino with other fabrics for smell.

paras: People wear merino as base layers, t-shirts and socks, often for gym, travel or long days, and re-wear pieces between washes.
Wikipedia notes heat and agitation shrink wool, and that a 2004 mulesing campaign led some retailers to drop Australian merino.

chain: Merino fabric worn next to skin
angle.text: Users wear merino wool next to skin as a fabric said to hold less odour, so clothes stay fresh between washes and smell better through the day. The claim is popular in grooming discussions.

lead: Merino is a fine, soft wool from the Merino sheep breed, widely used in sweaters, socks, T-shirts and base layers. In appearance and grooming discussions it is valued for how it feels and looks on the body: soft enough to wear against the skin, able to hold heat, and said to stay fresher-smelling between washes, which helps a person look and smell put together through a long day.

Wikipedia says the breed originated in the Iberian Peninsula in the High Middle Ages, and that its wool is generally under 24 microns in fibre diameter, graded from strong (23 to 24.5 microns) to ultra-fine (11.5 to 15 microns), with finer grades generally softer [1]. Wool in general readily absorbs moisture, up to nearly a third of its weight in water, and its crimped fibres trap air and retain heat [2].

Wearers say merino resists odour better than synthetics. Wikipedia's wool article says wool treated with lanolin is slightly antibacterial and resists odour build-up [2], and body odour is attributed to bacteria acting on skin secretions [3]. No study cited here directly compares merino with other fabrics for smell.

paras: Merino staples are commonly 65 to 100 mm long, and wool is graded from strong (23 to 24.5 microns) to ultra-fine (11.5 to 15 microns), with finer grades generally softer [1]. Fine merino is used for next-to-skin garments because it feels less prickly than coarser wool.

Wikipedia's wool article describes wool as readily absorbing moisture, with an outer fibre surface that repels water while the interior attracts it, and notes crimped fibres that hold air and retain heat; a small study of woollen underwear linked moisture absorption to fewer heat and sweat rashes [2]. Wool ignites at a higher temperature than cotton and some synthetics, spreads flame slowly and does not melt or drip [2].
Body odour is attributed to bacteria acting on skin secretions [3]. The wool article says lanolin-treated felted wool can resist the build-up of odour [2].

Spain kept the breed under monopoly, and by the mid-16th century its wool was considered equal to the finest English wools; flocks later spread across Europe, Australia and the Americas, and Merino reached Australia in the late 18th and early 19th centuries [1]. In 2004 several retailers stopped stocking Australian merino amid a campaign against mulesing, and New Zealand banned the practice in 2018 [1].

Merino is worn as base layers, T-shirts, socks, knitwear and jackets, and wearers report wearing items several times between washes. Wikipedia's laundry article notes that heat and agitation cause wool to shrink, so garments are commonly washed gently [4].
No studies found for merino clothing specifically. The wool article mentions a small study of woollen underwear and heat and sweat rashes [2].

lore.intro: Merino is discussed in grooming and style communities as a low-odour, temperature-regulating fabric for shirts and base layers.

claims.claim: Merino wool resists odour better than synthetics.
